newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Clinton faces strong criticism at Earth Summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton faces strong criticism at Earth Summit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton addresses the U.N. Earth Summit on Thursday with the United States the butt of criticism from all sides over its tarnished environmental record.

Clinton, originally slated to speak on the summit's first day on Monday, moved his speech to Thursday and then delayed it from the morning to the evening because he is attending funeral services for his much-loved great uncle in Arkansas.

The United States has been the main target of attack at the week-long meeting, from Europe over its refusal to set clear targets for cutting the gases that cause global warming, and from the Third World over declining aid.

Since the groundbreaking first Earth Summit five years ago in Rio de Janeiro, Washington has increased rather than stabilised its greenhouse gas emissions, slashed funds to help poor countries and failed to ratify an international treaty to protect biodiversity -- conservation of animal and plant life.
With such a record, environmentalists say the United States has lost its role as a leader who showed the world how to have cleaner air and water.

Many delegates say they dont expect much concrete response from Clinton to the criticism -- he stonewalled against European pressure at a Group of Seven summit in Denver last weekend to set targets for cutting greenhouse gases.
But Danish Environment Minister Svend Auken said Clinton must make a solid commitment to environmental issues.
"I expect a lot from Clinton. For the U.S. not to take the challenge of leadership would be entirely wrong.

"It would be wrong from an environment point of view, from a global point of view and especially from an American point of view if you leave the European Union as the driving force in international cooperation on the environment," he told Reuters on Thursday.
"I certainly hope he will go for a strong commitment on climate and some of the other issues. My expectations are high...he will do something, not just talk about the problems."

Clinton comes to the summit a day after defying big industries and backing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in setting tough new standards against air pollution. This could help Washington reduce its greenhouse gases.
But environmentalists said the move does not mean he should dodge another confrontation with polluting industries over global warming caused by burning fossil fuels.

"It doesn't take the pressure off for a strong position on climate change. The president has to be like a general practioner. He has to take care of the heart and he has to take care of the lungs," David Hawkins, of the Natural Resources Defence Council, said.

Administration officials blame Congress for their weak record on the environment, saying Republicans cut aid to developing countries and refused to ratify the biodiversity treaty or pass laws meeting goals for cutting greenhouse gases.

Officials say the United States cannot yield to European Union pressure to meet its target of cutting greenhouse gas eissions to 15 percent below 1990 levels by 2010, partly because they believe the public would not accept unpalatable changes in the U.S lifestyle needed to meet that goal.

Critics also say that five years after Rio, the Clinton administration lacks a coherent strategy on sustainable development -- the summit's underlying principle that economic growth can go hand-in-hand with environmental protection.
Clinton also has a checkered record on forest issues that make conservation groups sceptical of what kind of stance he will take at the summit.
Under pressure from Congress, he signed the widely lambasted "salvage logging rider" that gave timber companies access to old-growth wood under the guise of removing dead trees that could fuel fires.
He then scaled back the loggers' access, although green groups complain he acted too late to prevent serious loss of federal forests.
